newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu goes to West Bank amid settlement debate.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu goes to West Bank amid settlement debate.

text.p: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu dug Israeli roots deeper into the West Bank on Monday, laying the cornerstone to expand an Israeli college in a Jewish settlement.

In a speech at the College of Judea and Samaria, Netanyahu made no mention of any plans to halt the construction of 6,500 homes for Jews in Arab East Jerusalem, a project that has plunged Middle East peacemaking into deep crisis.

"I think the most important thing is to fortify our eastern border, the Jordan, and as a result of this to also keep in our hands direct responsibility for the Jordan Valley," Netanyahu told his right-wing Likud party faction.
"I also thought the matter of sovereign Jerusalem has to be understood from the outset -- that we have complete responsibility and sole sovereignty," Netanyahu said.

The Haaretz daily said Israel and the PLO might break an impasse in peace talks with a compromise that would allow Israel to continue building at the site on Jabel Abu Ghneim, or Har Homa, but at a "slow pace close to stoppage".
Netanyahu spokesman Shai Bazak, declining to discuss the details of the Haaretz report, said: "Work is proceeding at a regular pace" at the Jerusalem settlement. He did not elaborate.

In the settlement of Ariel, Netanyahu, who won election a year ago pledging to tighten Israel's hold on areas captured in the 1967 Middle East war, said Palestinians would one day study at the strategic studies centre under construction.

"That will happen when the Palestinian Authority understands that the road to peace means peace," he said after laying a cornerstone for the centre in the college, which has an Israeli student body of 4,500.
"It means stopping the murder of innocent people, or people who sell land to Jews," Netanyahu said, taking a swipe at the self-rule administration.
Netanyahu has alleged the Authority has ties to three recent killings of Arabs suspected of selling land to Jews. Palestinian security officials have denied involvement.
Prodded by Egyptian mediation, Israeli and Palestinian negotiators met formally for the first time in more than two months on Sunday in Cairo.

But Netanyahu, pressed by hawkish coalition partners who threaten to topple his slim six-vote majority in the 120-seat parliament, has declared he will resist Palestinian demands he curb settlement work as a condition for resuming talks.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said in Amman on Monday Israeli and Palestinian negotiators would resume talks on Thursday to revive the stalled peace talks.
"The Cairo meeting was a preliminary meeting and next Thursday we will continue the meeting," Arafat told reporters after talks with Jordan's Prime Minister Abdul Salam al-Majali.

Asked about reports that Israel had committed itself to a pledge to freeze settlement building as a condition to resume peace talks, Arafat said: "Unfortunately there are no Israeli promises to stop settlements."

Staking a biblical claim to the land of Israel, Netanyahu said the hill where Ariel, a settlement of 14,000 Jews, now stands had been barren for 2,000 years except for a scattering of Arabs who lived nearby.
He said that 20 years ago there had been "only wind" where apartment blocks now stand.
Palestinians say the Israeli home building at Jabel Abu Ghneim pre-empts talks on the fate of Jerusalem, one of a series of core issues the sides have pledged to settle by 1999.
Israel's Channel One television said on Sunday Netanyahu might be considering a clandestine end to Har Homa settlement.
Israeli right-wingers served notice that a halt to settlement work would spell the end of his government.

Israel claimed East Jerusalem as part of its capital after capturing it in the 1967 Middle East war. The claim is unrecognised internationally. The PLO sees East Jerusalem as the capital of a future Palestinian state.

Egypt, which considers itself an unofficial sponsor of the peace talks, has intensified its role in the peace crisis since a summit between Mubarak and Netanyahu last month. Analysts say it has even replaced the United States as the main mediator.
